opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the premise is a bit off: open-sourcing doesn't automatically get you to AGI faster. Community feedback is great for some things. Look at what happened with open-source RL libraries or the ecosystem around open-weight models: people find bugs, build tools, and explore weird directions no single company would. I really value that, and I've spent a lot of my own time on open-source projects.

But frontier model development is a different kind of problem. The bottleneck isn't that we lack ideas from outside or that nobody's reporting bugs. It's compute, data, infrastructure, and a very tight loop between research and engineering inside one team. Most of the community can't train a model at that scale, so publishing the weights doesn't really let them contribute to the next frontier model. It mostly lets them use and fine-tune the current one. That's valuable, but it's not the same as speeding up the core research.

Then there's the practical side. Training these models costs an enormous amount of money, and the company has to sustain that somehow. If you give away the thing you just spent billions on, it's hard to keep funding the next run. Whether you like it or not, that's part of why things are set up this way.

And the part people sometimes dismiss, but which I think is real, is safety and misuse. Once you release weights, you can't take them back. If a capability turns out to be dangerous, or a safeguard can be easily stripped out, there's no patch. A closed model lets you monitor usage, roll things back, and learn how people actually use it before deciding what's safe to release more broadly.

That said, I don't think it's black and white. OpenAI has released some open-weight models, and I think there's a reasonable middle ground: share research insights, tools, and smaller models, and be more careful at the very frontier. Reasonable people disagree about where that line should be, and I think that debate is healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says releasing weights lets others use and fine-tune the current model, but does not claim competitors would immediately catch up or erase the developer’s lead.

r002.rationale: It does not mention competitors keeping their own improvements closed-source.

r003.rationale: It says giving away a model that cost billions to build makes it hard to keep funding the next training run.

r004.rationale: It discusses funding, safety, and misuse, but does not frame staying closed-source as protection against actors pursuing profit instead of benefiting humanity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing first, because I don't think it's really a question of "closed is good, open is bad." It's more about what you're optimizing for at each stage.

Community feedback is genuinely valuable. I spent years in the open-source world before joining OpenAI, and I've seen firsthand how a thousand people poking at your code find bugs and ideas you'd never find on your own. So I'm not going to pretend that's worthless.

But there are a few things that make frontier models different from a typical open-source library. The first is that the marginal gain from community feedback on a library is mostly about code quality, whereas with a frontier model the hard part isn't the code. It's the data, the compute, the infrastructure, and the thousands of small decisions in training that nobody outside can reproduce anyway. Releasing weights doesn't actually let the community iterate on the thing that matters most. They can fine-tune, they can study it, but they can't retrain it.

The second is safety, and I know people roll their eyes at that word, but it's real in a practical sense. Once weights are out, they're out forever. You can't patch them. If you later discover a capability or a failure mode that's dangerous, there's no recall. With an API, you can monitor, you can rate-limit, you can update the model, you can actually learn from how people misuse it and fix it. That feedback loop is honestly a form of community feedback too, just a controlled one.

The third thing is just economics. Training these systems costs an enormous amount, and someone has to pay for the next one. If you give away the result for free, you're relying on the goodwill of whoever has the compute, and that's not a stable way to get to AGI either.

So my view is that it's not binary. OpenAI has open-sourced things, evaluation tooling, smaller models, research papers that other labs build on. The frontier stuff stays closed for now, and I think that's a defensible tradeoff while the stakes are this high and the capabilities are moving this fast. If things stabilize, I'd expect the line to move. It's already moved quite a bit in the open-weight ecosystem, and I think that's healthy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost of training and the limits of releasing weights, but does not say competitors could immediately catch up or erase OpenAI’s lead.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss competitors keeping improvements to an open model closed-source.

r003.rationale: It says training costs enormously, someone must pay for the next model, and giving away the result is not a stable path to AGI, communicating a concern about sustaining funding.

r004.rationale: The response cites safety, economics, and the stakes of frontier development, but does not frame closure as protection against actors prioritizing profit over benefiting humanity.

astra-6.text:
I’d question the idea that OpenAI needs to remain entirely closed-source. Community feedback can help uncover flaws, improve safety, and bring in ideas that a single organization might miss. But that doesn’t necessarily mean every capability should be released openly as soon as it exists.

The strongest argument for keeping some things closed is that releasing model weights can be difficult to reverse. If a model has dangerous capabilities, you lose some ability to control access or respond to misuse. At the same time, being closed doesn’t automatically make a system safe, and it makes independent scrutiny harder.

So I’d favor a more selective approach: share research, enable independent evaluations, and release models when the risks are manageable. The question should be what level of openness is appropriate for a particular system, rather than whether openness or secrecy is always the right answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d question the premise that OpenAI needs to remain closed-source. Community feedback could help uncover problems and improve the technology. But that doesn’t automatically mean releasing everything is the best choice at every stage. Some capabilities could be difficult to safeguard once they’re widely available.

For me, the question is what to share, when, and with what protections. You can invite outside scrutiny through research, evaluations, and controlled access while being more cautious about releasing model weights. But keeping those weights closed shouldn’t mean avoiding accountability. If a company argues that openness is too risky, it should explain those risks clearly and make room for independent scrutiny.
